title: A friend at midnight (Luke 11:5–13)
hook: a friend knocks for bread at midnight and keeps knocking

segments.voice: Yesterday, a disciple watched Jesus pray and said, show us how. Your line was teach us. Who did you ask to teach you something? Day five hundred forty-four.

Straight after giving the prayer, Jesus tells a story, and it starts with a problem every village knew. It's midnight. A friend has turned up after a long journey, tired and hungry. And the cupboard is empty. In that world, a guest was the whole village's honor; you couldn't send him to bed with nothing. Bread was usually baked in the morning, so by midnight it's gone. There is one option. Walk down the dark lane to a neighbor's house, where the door is barred and the whole family is asleep, and knock.

In the King James Bible, the man at the door calls out: "Friend, lend me three loaves; For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him?" And from inside comes the answer every parent understands: "Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee." Houses were often one room. Getting up means unbarring the door and waking everyone. But the knocking doesn't stop. Jesus says the neighbor will get up, not because they're friends, but "because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth." Importunity is the old English word. The Greek is anaideia, and it means shamelessness, a nerve that doesn't care how it looks. Scholars actually argue about whose shamelessness it is. Most read it as the knocker's, refusing to give up. Some read it as the sleeper's, who gets up to avoid the shame of failing a neighbor. Either way, here's the turn. The story isn't saying God is a grumpy neighbor who has to be nagged. It works by contrast: if even a sleepy friend gets up at midnight, how much more will God. Then come the words: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." And Luke ends with a twist of his own. Matthew says the Father gives good things. Luke says: "how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" Not just bread, but God's own presence, for anyone bold enough to keep knocking.
screen: `TROUBLE ME NOT: THE DOOR IS SHUT.`
`NOT A GRUMPY GOD: HOW MUCH MORE.`
then, large: `KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask boldly, like a friend at a friend's door. Settle and breathe. Think of one thing you need, really need, that you've stopped asking for because it felt embarrassing, or greedy, or too late. Let it come to mind plainly. If you pray, you can ask for it in your own words, the way you'd ask a friend, without polishing the request. Then ask again. If you don't pray, simply let yourself admit the need without apologizing for it. Notice what it feels like to stop pretending you're fine. The bell holds the time.
A friend at midnight. A man knocks on a barred door for three loaves and keeps knocking, and the story says: how much more will God give.
Your line: shamelessly ask. Today, ask one person for help you've been too proud to request, and don't apologize for asking. Day five hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Many Christians bring the same request to God again and again, in personal prayer, in prayer lists kept by churches, and in intercessions during Sunday worship, reading this story as permission to keep asking.

original.note: Greek: shamelessness, nerve. the King James Bible says importunity.

trapdoor: what you thought: keep nagging God and eventually God gives in.
what it means: if even a sleepy neighbor gets up at midnight for a friend, how much more will God give to those who ask.
what a scholar hears: anaideia means shamelessness, and scholars debate whether it belongs to the knocker or to the sleeper avoiding the shame of failing a neighbor.
